design_detail: Systematic review with random-effects single-group (proportion) meta-analysis of the share of people with a substance use disorder (alcohol, heroin or several substances) who were in remission at the last follow-up of observational cohorts published 2000–2015 with at least three years of follow-up, or with lifetime cumulative probabilities. 21 cohorts (12 alcohol, 4 heroin, 5 polysubstance). Two rates were pooled: a 'standard' rate (people in remission at final follow-up divided by those who reached it) and a 'conservative' rate (the same people divided by everyone at baseline, counting deaths and losses as not remitted). Also reported: annualized remission rates under a constant-rate model (PEARRs), subgroup analyses, univariate meta-regressions and trim-and-fill. No protocol registration is mentioned.
can_establish: The range of remission proportions reported by long-term cohorts of people with alcohol, heroin or polysubstance use disorders published 2000–2015, mostly recruited through treatment, and how strongly those proportions depend on how losses are counted and on the length of follow-up.
cannot_establish: A remission rate for people with substance use disorders in general (15 of 21 cohorts were clinical samples, and follow-up ran from 3 to 50 years), the chance of remission within any given period (the pooled proportions mix very different follow-up lengths), whether remission depends on treatment (treatment during follow-up was not analysed), or how often remission occurs among people who never reach treatment (two general-population cohorts only).

sample.recruitment: Database search of Medline, PubMed, EMBASE and PsycINFO, hand search of 19 addiction journals chosen by experts, and reference lists; studies published January 2000 to December 2015, from OECD countries, in English or French (PDF pp. 2–3, Methods › 2.1).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: observational studies of people with an SUD (abuse or dependence) at baseline, with follow-up of three years or more and two or more data collections, or lifetime remission with cumulative probability estimates; participants at least 18 at final follow-up; remission defined over at least six months. Excluded: cohorts in which not everyone had an SUD at baseline; studies limited to particular groups (homeless people, indigenous peoples, veterans, people with medical conditions such as pregnant women); trials, studies of experimental treatments and of methadone or buprenorphine programmes; for cohorts published several times, all but the longest follow-up (PDF pp. 2–3, Methods › 2.1; Fig. 1, PDF p. 4).
sample.demographics: Across the 21 cohorts: follow-up 3 to 50 years (mean 17, median 13); baseline N 86 to 5,719 (mean 1,018, median 613); mean age 33 at baseline and 48 at last follow-up; on average 70% men in 16 cohorts and only men in the other 5; 34% to 98% White (10 cohorts reporting); unemployment 16% to 86% (10 cohorts); 10% to 89% with co-occurring mental disorders (7 cohorts); 24% to 100% involved in criminal activity (8 cohorts) (PDF pp. 4, 7, Results › 3.1). 13 cohorts were from the US (editors' count from Table 1 and the text).
sample.attrition: Review level: not applicable. Within cohorts, retention ranged from 21% to 96% (mean 67%) counting deaths as losses and from 47% to 98% (mean 80%) excluding deaths (PDF p. 4, Results › 3.1, 1st paragraph).
sample.selection_effects: Mostly treatment-recruited cohorts: 15 clinical, 4 community and 2 general-population samples (both from the US NESARC survey) (PDF p. 11); all four heroin cohorts were treatment samples, one of them a compulsory, court-ordered treatment programme (Table 1 footnote g, PDF p. 6). The authors expect population samples to show better outcomes (PDF p. 11). Excluding veterans, trials and opioid-agonist programmes, and keeping only the longest follow-up, shapes which cohorts entered. One cohort entered here as a clinical sample, Moos and Moos (2007), is drawn from the source cohort that Mellor et al. (2019, pp. 64–66) treat as initially untreated people, seen after a single detox episode or at an information and referral centre.

exposure.measurement: The 'exposure' is having an SUD at baseline, as diagnosed in each cohort: DSM-III, DSM-III-R, DSM-IV, ICD-10, or study instruments and records (Alcohol Use Scale, Drinking Problem Index, Augmented Addiction Severity Index, Natural History Interview, screening interviews, clinical records) (Table 1, PDF pp. 5–6). The authors note that eight cohorts relied on self-reported SUD (PDF p. 11). 14 cohorts included any SUD (abuse and/or dependence), 7 dependence only (PDF p. 4).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not applicable. Duration of the disorder before remission was reported by 8 cohorts (see key findings); the authors note that duration before entry was rarely recorded (PDF p. 11).
exposure.polysubstance: Five cohorts were classed as polysubstance. In two of them, separate substance-specific estimates were merged into one rate without a stated method: Hser et al. (2008), 0.33 heroin, 0.80 methamphetamine, 0.87 cocaine, entered as 0.660; Lopez-Quintero et al. (2011), lifetime estimates for alcohol, cannabis and cocaine, entered as 0.957 (Fig. 4 notes, PDF p. 10). The authors note that cohorts rarely checked whether people in remission from one substance had moved to another (PDF p. 11).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Remission meant not meeting abuse or dependence criteria for at least six months at the final follow-up (PDF p. 1): minimum 6 months in 5 cohorts, 12 months in 12, 5 to 10 years in 4; 7 cohorts required abstinence and 14 accepted controlled use (PDF p. 4).

comparison.controls: None: a single-group meta-analysis of proportions. All comparisons are between cohorts (subgroups and meta-regressions), not within them.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Characteristics not tested as moderators, which the authors say could explain the heterogeneity: criminal activity, unemployment, social support, co-occurring mental disorders and treatment received over time (PDF p. 11); duration of the disorder before entry was rarely recorded (PDF p. 11).

outcomes.instruments: Each cohort's own remission assessment (Table 1). Two summary measures defined by the reviewers: the standard rate (people in continuous remission of more than six months at final follow-up, divided by those reaching final follow-up, excluding the dead, the lost and those no longer eligible) and the conservative rate (the same numerator divided by the whole baseline sample) (PDF p. 3, Methods › 2.3.1). PEARR: the sample-size-weighted mean of −ln(1−b)/c across cohorts, where b is the remission proportion and c the years of follow-up (PDF p. 3, Methods › 2.3.3); for the lifetime cohort, c was set at 40 years (Table 1 footnote n, PDF p. 6).
outcomes.validity_norms: Included studies were 'critically appraised for inclusion' with questions adapted from the Critical Appraisal Skills Programme; no study-level appraisal results are reported (PDF p. 3, Methods › 2.2).
outcomes.operationalization: Remission is status at the final follow-up only: a person abstinent for most of the follow-up who relapsed in its last six months counts as not remitted, as the authors note (PDF p. 11). Remission definitions ranged from abstinence to controlled use, and minimum durations from 6 months to 10 years (PDF p. 4).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. Two pooled outcomes (standard and conservative rates), each tested in 5 subgroup comparisons and 4 univariate meta-regressions (18 moderator tests), at alpha 0.05 'given the exploratory nature' of the analyses (PDF p. 3).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable. Two reviewers screened titles and abstracts independently, with a third resolving disagreements (agreement 96% on a 10% sample); full texts were read and data extracted independently by two team members (PDF p. 3, Methods › 2.2).

analysis.effect_sizes: Random-effects pooling of proportions weighted by inverse variance (Comprehensive Meta-Analysis). Standard rate 54.4% (95% CI 42.1 to 66.2), study values 19.6% to 95.7%, weighted mean follow-up 17.9 years (SD 14.0), I2 99.4%, tau2 1.3, Q 3337.3 on 20 df; leave-one-out 50.1% to 56.4%; PEARR 9.1% (8.4 to 9.8). Conservative rate 35.0% (25.2 to 46.4) in the text (0.351, 0.252 to 0.464 in Fig. 4), study values 15.5% to 95.7%, weighted mean follow-up 16.9 years (SD 13.4), I2 99.5%, tau2 1.2, Q 3890.7 on 20 df; leave-one-out 30.9% to 36.3%; without the lifetime cohort 30.9% (26.1 to 36.1), I2 97.7%; PEARR 6.8% (6.3 to 7.4) (PDF p. 7; Fig. 4, PDF p. 10). No prediction intervals. Trim-and-fill: standard 0.60 (0.47 to 0.71), conservative 0.48 (0.38 to 0.59) (PDF p. 7). Editors' calculation: the PEARRs reproduce from Fig. 4 and Table 1 (9.1% weighting by final N, 6.8% by baseline N), but at a constant 9.1% or 6.8% per year cumulative remission after 17.9 years would be about 80% or 70%, whereas the pooled proportions imply about 4.4% and 2.6% per year (−ln(1−p)/t); the two summaries are not consistent under the constant-rate assumption the PEARR makes.
analysis.covariates: Univariate meta-regressions (follow-up duration, proportion male, age in 18 cohorts, retention in 20 cohorts) and subgroup analyses (substance, treatment at baseline, diagnosis, remission definition, remission duration), each tested separately; no multivariable model (PDF p. 3; Tables 2 and 3, PDF pp. 8, 10).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is mentioned; the review states that it followed PRISMA (PDF p. 2).
analysis.selective_reporting: The funnel plots are not published ('available upon request', PDF p. 7); study-level appraisal results are not reported; the search strategy is described only by example keywords (PDF p. 2); how the substance-specific estimates of two cohorts were combined is not stated (Fig. 4 notes, PDF p. 10).
analysis.power: Not formally addressed; subgroups contain 4 to 15 cohorts and meta-regressions 18 to 21, and the authors say the small number of studies makes the non-significant moderator results hard to interpret (PDF p. 11).

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 21 mostly treatment-recruited cohorts followed for 3 to 50 years, between about a fifth and almost all participants were in remission at the last follow-up; pooled, 54% of those followed up (35% of everyone enrolled, counting deaths and losses as not remitted), with heterogeneity above 99%. Standard rates were higher in cohorts with longer follow-up and lower retention; no subgroup difference reached significance by substance, treatment at baseline (51% treated vs 62% not, standard rate), diagnosis, remission definition or remission duration.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and conclusion say the results support the view that SUDs are more likely to be 'chronic' or long-term disorders for a substantial number of people, that the PEARRs projected few cases of remission in any given year, and that treatment geared to chronicity such as assertive community treatment and intensive case management should be more available (PDF pp. 1, 12). Gaps: (1) a pooled proportion over follow-ups of 3 to 50 years describes no particular time point, and the review's own meta-regression shows the proportion rising with follow-up; (2) at the reported 6.8% to 9.1% a year, half of a cohort would remit in about 7.6 to 10.2 years (ln 2 divided by the rate; editors' calculation), which does not obviously mean 'few cases'; (3) 15 of 21 cohorts were clinical samples, whose course the authors expect to be worse than the population's (PDF p. 11), so the chronicity reading applies mainly to people who reached treatment; (4) the service recommendations are not tested by any analysis; (5) the Discussion restates 17.9 and 16.9 years of follow-up as years of substance use or consumption (PDF p. 7), and the conclusion that most people used for at least 14 years before remission (PDF p. 12) is not supported by the eight durations reported, several of which are under 10 years (Table 1; PDF p. 7). The limitations section is candid about heterogeneity, definitions and the small number of cohorts (PDF p. 11).

timeline.event: Calabria et al., systematic review of prospective studies of remission from amphetamine, cannabis, cocaine or opioid dependence; the source of this review's three-year minimum and annualized-rate method, cited here as reporting 5% (cocaine) to 22% (opioid) remission a year (PDF pp. 2–3, 7; General list #21; not read for this card).
White's analysis of 415 reports from 1868 to 2011, cited here as finding that about half of participants had remitted by the final follow-up (PDF p. 2; not read for this card).

Heyman, synthesis of national surveys, cited here as finding half of people with an alcohol use disorder in remission 16 years after onset and four years for cocaine (PDF p. 10; General list #23; not read for this card).
This review: the first systematic review and meta-analysis of remission across alcohol and illicit-drug use disorders, by the authors' account (PDF pp. 2, 11).

Mellor et al., systematic review of untreated remission from alcohol problems, showing how estimates depend on the starting sample and on definitions; it does not cite this review, and it treats the source cohort of Moos and Moos (2007) as initially untreated.

replication.where_it_stands: The pooled figures are best cited as a range for long-term, mostly treatment-recruited cohorts: about a third (counting everyone enrolled) to about half (counting those followed up) were in remission at a last follow-up averaging 17 years. They are not an estimate of remission among all people with substance use disorders, among whom general-population cohorts, two of them here, are expected to show more remission; the primary cohorts should be cited for figures specific to a substance or time point.

funding.funder: Partly funded by a grant from the National Institute of Excellence in Health and Social Services, Quebec, Canada (Institut National d'Excellence en Santé et en Services Sociaux, INESSS); the funder had no role in study design or data collection for the review (PDF p. 12).
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors report no conflicts of interest, including financial interests or affiliations relevant to the manuscript (PDF p. 12).
funding.affiliations_note: Authors from McGill University (Department of Psychiatry; Douglas Mental Health University Institute), Université du Québec à Trois-Rivières, Université Laval and three Quebec addiction rehabilitation centres; four of the seven authors are affiliated with addiction rehabilitation centres, and the review closes by recommending more chronic-care services. Recorded as a flag for closer reading of the recommendations, not as a reason to discount the results.

what_would_settle_it: General-population cohorts that identify people when they first meet criteria, reassess them with a standard diagnostic interview at fixed intervals for ten years or more, record treatment as it happens and analyse time to first sustained remission and to relapse with survival methods that account for deaths and losses; or an individual-participant meta-analysis of existing cohorts using one remission definition and time-to-event methods, reporting treated and never-treated people separately.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Population (people with an SUD at baseline), outcome (remission of at least six months at final follow-up), minimum follow-up and designs are specified (PDF pp. 1–3).
No protocol or registration is mentioned; PRISMA was followed (PDF p. 2).
Observational cohorts only; trials and studies of experimental or substitution treatment excluded because their selection favours atypical participants exposed to best practice (PDF p. 3).

Four databases, hand search of 19 journals and reference lists, search ending December 2015 for a paper received in March 2016; but the strategy is given only as example keywords, the English-or-French restriction is not justified, and grey literature and non-peer-reviewed reports were excluded (PDF pp. 2, 11). Judged 'no' under item 4 as written, as the project applies it to unjustified language limits (decision p-amstar2-item4).
Two reviewers screened independently with a third for disagreements (96% agreement on 10% of records), and two read the full texts (PDF p. 3).
Two team members extracted independently with a standardized form (PDF p. 3).

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: Fig. 1 gives exclusion reasons with counts for the 98 excluded full texts, but no list of the excluded studies (PDF p. 4).

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Table 1 gives country, N at baseline and follow-up, retention, age, sex, ethnicity, population, diagnosis, instruments, follow-up length, remission definition and duration of the disorder; treatment received during follow-up is not described (PDF pp. 5–6).

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: Studies were appraised only as a gate for inclusion with questions adapted from CASP; no domain-level judgments or results are reported, and confounding, selection and measurement were not assessed study by study (PDF p. 3).

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported

domains.note: Inverse-variance random-effects pooling is a suitable technique, but combining was not justified for an outcome that depends on time: proportions observed after 3 to 50 years and a model-based lifetime probability (placed at 40 years) were pooled into one figure, the review's own meta-regression shows follow-up explaining part of the variation, two cohorts' substance-specific estimates were merged into one value by an unstated method, and no prediction interval is given despite I2 above 99% (PDF pp. 3, 6–7, 10).

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: No study-level risk of bias was assessed. The conservative-versus-standard comparison and the retention meta-regression address attrition only (PDF pp. 3, 7).

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: The discussion weighs attrition (actual remission likely between the two rates), the predominance of clinical samples, self-reported SUD in eight cohorts and small final samples, and asks for caution (PDF pp. 7, 11).
Q, I2 and tau2 reported; subgroup analyses and meta-regressions explored sources; residual heterogeneity is acknowledged as unexplained (PDF pp. 7, 10–11).

Funnel plots and trim-and-fill, with impact discussed (PDF pp. 7, 11). The funnel plots are not published, and the limitations both say the adjusted estimates may be higher and that reporting bias seems unlikely; for single-group proportions the meaning of funnel asymmetry is uncertain.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: Funding and a no-conflict statement are printed (PDF p. 12).

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Five critical items are not met (2, 4, 7, 9 and 11), which gives critically low confidence under AMSTAR 2. The decisive weaknesses for the encyclopedia are not procedural: the headline proportions pool cohorts followed for 3 to 50 years and mostly recruited through treatment, the lifetime NESARC estimate sits beside observed proportions, and no study-level appraisal was done. The review may be cited for the range of remission proportions in long-term cohorts (about 20% to 96% among those followed up), for the effect of counting losses (35% vs 54%), for the finding that standard rates rose with follow-up length and fell with retention, for the absence of a detectable difference by substance, treatment at baseline or remission definition, and as a pointer to the primary cohorts. It should not be cited for a general remission rate, for an annual chance of remission, or for the claim that most people use for at least 14 years before remission.

key_findings.finding: Search and selection: Medline, PubMed, EMBASE and PsycINFO, a hand search of 19 addiction journals and reference lists, for studies published January 2000 to December 2015 in OECD countries, in English or French; 8,855 records screened, 119 full texts assessed and 21 cohorts included (12 alcohol, 4 heroin, 5 polysubstance). Of the 98 full texts excluded, 49 gave no remission data at final follow-up, 18 included people without an SUD at baseline, 15 had follow-up under three years, 4 were from outside the OECD, 4 defined remission over less than six months, 4 assessed interventions, 2 concerned special populations and 2 duplicated a cohort.
key_findings.locator: Methods › 2.1 (PDF pp. 2–3); Results › 3.1, 1st paragraph (PDF p. 3); Fig. 1 (PDF p. 4; an image, counts read on the rendered page)
key_findings.note: The Results text gives 8,885 records; the abstract and Fig. 1 give 8,855 (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Included cohorts: follow-up 3 to 50 years (mean 17, median 13); baseline N 86 to 5,719 (mean 1,018, median 613); retention 21% to 96% counting deaths (mean 67%) and 47% to 98% excluding them (mean 80%); mean age 33 at baseline and 48 at last follow-up; on average 70% men in 16 cohorts and only men in 5; 14 cohorts any SUD and 7 dependence only; remission required for at least 6 months (5 cohorts), 12 months (12) or 5 to 10 years (4); 7 cohorts required abstinence, 14 accepted controlled use. 15 cohorts were clinical, 4 community and 2 general-population samples.
key_findings.locator: Results › 3.1, 1st to 3rd paragraphs (PDF pp. 3–4, figures on p. 4); Discussion, 7th paragraph (starting PDF p. 10; sample types on p. 11)

key_findings.finding: Standard remission rate (people in remission at final follow-up among those who reached it): study values 19.6% to 95.7%; pooled 54.4% (95% CI 42.1 to 66.2) after a weighted mean follow-up of 17.9 years (SD 14.0); I2 99.4%, tau2 1.3, Q 3337.3 (df 20); removing one cohort at a time gave 50.1% to 56.4%; annualized pooled rate (PEARR) 9.1% (8.4 to 9.8).

Conservative remission rate (same people in remission divided by everyone enrolled): study values 15.5% to 95.7%; pooled 35.0% (95% CI 25.2 to 46.4) after a weighted mean follow-up of 16.9 years (SD 13.4); I2 99.5%, tau2 1.2, Q 3890.7 (df 20); leave-one-out 30.9% to 36.3%; without the lifetime NESARC cohort (Lopez-Quintero et al., 2011) 30.9% (26.1 to 36.1), I2 97.7%; PEARR 6.8% (6.3 to 7.4). The authors judge that actual remission probably lies between the two rates.
key_findings.locator: Results › 3.3, 2nd paragraph; Discussion, 3rd paragraph; Fig. 4 (PDF p. 10)
key_findings.note: Fig. 4 prints the conservative pooled estimate as 0.351 (0.252 to 0.464).

key_findings.finding: Subgroups (Table 2), none significant. Standard rate: alcohol 0.517 (0.354 to 0.676), heroin 0.540 (0.269 to 0.789), polysubstance 0.609 (0.359 to 0.813), p 0.833; treatment at baseline 0.511 (15 cohorts) vs none 0.624 (6 cohorts), p 0.421; any SUD 0.464 (14) vs dependence only 0.695 (7), p 0.060; controlled use or abstinence 0.570 vs abstinence only 0.491, p 0.568; remission of 6 months 0.428, 12 months 0.597, 5 years or more 0.528, p 0.570. Conservative rate: alcohol 0.298, heroin 0.275, polysubstance 0.509 (p 0.157); treatment at baseline 0.382 vs none 0.279 (p 0.388); any SUD 0.289 vs dependence only 0.489 (p 0.081).
key_findings.note: Table 2 footnotes: 'treatment at baseline' means all or most people were in treatment at baseline; two of the six cohorts without treatment at baseline were population samples in which some people were in treatment. Treatment during follow-up was not analysed.

key_findings.finding: Univariate meta-regressions (Table 3): the standard rate was higher in cohorts with longer follow-up (B 0.046 per year, SE 0.016, 95% CI 0.014 to 0.08, R2 analog 0.30, p 0.004) and lower retention (B −1.975, SE 0.821, −3.583 to −0.367, R2 analog 0.06, p 0.016), and unrelated to proportion male (p 0.754) or age (18 cohorts, p 0.412). No characteristic predicted the conservative rate (follow-up p 0.235; retention p 0.060; male p 0.262; age p 0.446).
key_findings.note: The scale of B (probably the logit of the proportion) is not stated.

key_findings.finding: Funnel plots, not published, were described as asymmetric with more cohorts below the mean; trim-and-fill trimmed 3 cohorts for the standard rate (adjusted 0.60, 0.47 to 0.71) and 9 for the conservative rate (adjusted 0.48, 0.38 to 0.59).

Duration of the disorder before remission, reported by 8 cohorts: alcohol 9.6 (Gual), 11 (Mann), 13.6 (Penick) and 19 years (Vaillant); regular heroin use 22 years (Hser 2007); polysubstance median 27 years (Dennis); about 4 years of injecting before remission (Galai); in NESARC, half of people with alcohol, cannabis and cocaine dependence remitted about 14, 6 and 5 years after onset (Lopez-Quintero et al., 2011).
key_findings.locator: Table 1, last column and footnote o (PDF pp. 5–6); Results › 3.2 (PDF p. 7)
key_findings.note: Values as printed in Table 1. The text of 3.2 attributes the 11 years to Moos and Moos (2007), for whom Table 1 prints NA, and gives the NESARC medians as 6 years for alcohol and 14 for cannabis, the reverse of Table 1 (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: The lifetime NESARC cohort (5,719 people) entered both analyses as 0.957 (0.951 to 0.962); its components are given as 0.91 alcohol, 0.97 cannabis and 0.998 cocaine for the standard rate, and as 37%, 66% and 76% for the conservative rate; for the PEARR its follow-up was set at 40 years. The multi-sample cohort of Hser et al. (2008) entered as 0.660 from 0.33 heroin, 0.80 methamphetamine and 0.87 cocaine.
key_findings.locator: Table 1 footnote n (PDF p. 6); Fig. 4 and notes b to d (PDF p. 10; an image, values read at 300 dpi)

key_findings.finding: Limitations stated by the authors: few cohorts; trials, experimental studies and non-peer-reviewed reports excluded; OECD countries and English or French only, mostly US samples except for heroin; remission definitions from abstinence to controlled use and durations from 6 months to 10 years; status at final follow-up only, so people abstinent for most of the follow-up but relapsing near its end count as not remitted; eight cohorts used self-reported SUD; final samples of 41 to 129 people in a third of the cohorts; possible switching to another substance not checked.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 7th paragraph (starting PDF p. 10; self-reported SUD and small final samples on p. 11) and 9th paragraph (substance switching, PDF p. 11); 4.1 Limitations (PDF p. 11)

key_findings.finding: Conclusions: a third to a half of people with SUDs achieved remission after a mean follow-up of 17 years; annual remission of one person in ten to one in 15; the findings are said to support the view that SUDs are 'chronic' or long-term disorders for a significant number of people, and chronic-care management, assertive community treatment and intensive case management are recommended.

reporting_issues.issue: The number of records screened is 8,855 in the abstract and Fig. 1 (171 + 10,921 − 2,237 duplicates) but 8,885 in the Results text.

The Discussion restates the weighted mean follow-up (17.9 and 16.9 years) as years of substance use or consumption, saying 54% were in remission after 18 years of use and 35% after 17 years of consumption.
reporting_issues.consequence: Follow-up time is not duration of use; the figures must not be quoted as years of use before remission.

reporting_issues.issue: Section 3.2 gives the NESARC times to half remission as 5 years (cocaine), 6 (alcohol) and 14 (cannabis); Table 1 footnote o gives 14 (alcohol), 6 (cannabis) and 5 (cocaine). Section 3.2 also attributes 11 years of active drinking before remission to Moos and Moos (2007), for whom Table 1 prints NA; Table 1 gives 11 years for Mann et al. (2005).
reporting_issues.consequence: Alcohol and cannabis are swapped in one of the two places, and one study attribution is wrong; the primary paper is needed before quoting substance-specific times to remission.

reporting_issues.issue: The conclusion that the mean consumption period before remission was at least 14 years for most people (PDF p. 12), and the Discussion's 14 years for more than two thirds (PDF p. 9), cannot be derived from the eight durations reported (4 to 27 years, several under 10), which also measure different things (mean, median, years of injecting, time to half remission).
reporting_issues.consequence: The 14-year figure should not be cited.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion says cohorts of any SUD showed better standard remission than dependence-only cohorts (PDF p. 10); Table 2 shows the reverse (0.464 for any SUD vs 0.695 for dependence only).
reporting_issues.consequence: The direction of the (non-significant) diagnosis difference is misreported in the text; use Table 2.

reporting_issues.issue: In Table 2, the conservative-rate subgroups by substance have narrow, non-overlapping intervals (alcohol 0.287 to 0.309; heroin 0.253 to 0.298; polysubstance 0.497 to 0.520), which by the Methods' own rule would indicate significant differences, yet Q is 3.707 (p 0.157) and the text reports no significant factor; the intervals are far narrower than the random-effects intervals elsewhere. The conservative 'treatment at baseline' row also gives 2 df for two groups, while its p value (0.388) corresponds to 1 df.
reporting_issues.consequence: The conservative-rate substance intervals appear to come from a different model or to be misprinted; they should not be cited.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion gives the subgroup estimates for alcohol, heroin and polysubstance as 51.7%, 54.0% and 60.0% (PDF p. 11); Table 2 gives 0.517, 0.540 and 0.609.

Fig. 4 shows 0.957 for the lifetime NESARC cohort in the conservative panel, but its footnote gives component rates of 37%, 66% and 76%, which cannot yield 0.957; how either panel's components were combined is not stated.
reporting_issues.consequence: The conservative value for the cohort with the largest single influence on that estimate cannot be verified.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 prints a retention of 79% for Delucchi et al. (2004), whose Ns are 1,599 at baseline and 1,094 at final follow-up, and NA for Cranford et al. (2014). By the editors' calculations, Delucchi's Ns give 68%, as does the ratio of its conservative to standard rate in Fig. 4 (0.183/0.268), and Cranford's Ns give 78%.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the retention column cannot be relied on for single cohorts.

reporting_issues.issue: Results 3.1 gives final follow-up samples of 45 to 1,797 people for the 20 prospective cohorts (PDF p. 4); Table 1 lists 41 for Vaillant (2003), as does the Discussion (41 to 129, PDF p. 11).

Table 3 prints Q 0.20 for proportion male (standard rate), where B and SE (0.506, 1.612) give about 0.10 and p 0.754 corresponds to that smaller value; the confidence-interval columns are both headed 'Lower limit'.
The index under Fig. 2 omits cohorts 6 (Noda et al., 2001) and 12 (Vaillant, 2003), which are plotted; Okruhlica et al. (2002) has an age range printed in reverse order (26.3 to 16.7).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; Fig. 3's index identifies the two cohorts.

reporting_issues.issue: The annualized rates (PEARRs) assume a constant yearly rate and weight cohorts by sample size, so large cohorts with short follow-up dominate. By the editors' calculation, at 9.1% or 6.8% a year cumulative remission after 17.9 years would be about 80% or 70%, far above the pooled 54% and 35%.
reporting_issues.consequence: The PEARRs and the pooled proportions are not mutually consistent; neither should be quoted as the yearly chance of remission.

verification.source_read: In-press PDF ('Article in press', Drug and Alcohol Dependence (2016), 14 pages numbered 1–14, first page unnumbered); its pages differ from the version of record (vol. 168, pp. 293–306 in the reference record), so anchors give PDF pages. All pages read; Tables 1–3 and Figs. 1–4 checked on rendered pages (Tables 1 and 2 printed sideways, read at 220 dpi; Fig. 4 study values and Table 3 read at 300 dpi). Funnel plots not published (available from the authors on request); no supplement.
